btd: the transport-independent half, with no radio

First slice of the BLE front door (architecture.md §4.1). `btd` is a transport
adapter and owns no state — if provisioning or config lived here, every other
service would depend on it and an SDK would absurdly have to go through
Bluetooth to set a robot's name.

So the design is a pipe: a GATT service with two characteristics, write
`request` and notify `response`, carrying **the same NDJSON JSON-RPC lines as
every other transport**. Adding a protocol method then needs no code here beyond
one line in the routing table. Per-method characteristics were the alternative —
browsable in a generic BLE app, but a second dialect of the same API, and a poor
fit for `update.subscribe`'s notification stream.

Two modules, both testable without hardware, which is where the logic actually
lives:

`framing` — reassembly and chunking. There is deliberately **no framing header**:
the newline that already separates NDJSON messages is the frame delimiter in both
directions. That is safe rather than lucky, because serde_json escapes a newline
inside a string as `\n`, so a raw 0x0A never appears inside a serialised object —
the same property that makes NDJSON work on the unix socket. A length prefix
would be a BLE-only dialect every client had to implement; instead a phone does
what robotctl does, write bytes and read until newline. Reassembly is capped at
8 KiB because the buffer is reachable by anyone in radio range.

`route` — which calls BLE may make, and which socket answers them. One table for
both, since they are the same question. The match over `proto::Call` is
**exhaustive on purpose**: adding a variant fails the build here, so a new method
cannot reach the radio because someone forgot this file existed. A `_ => None`
wildcard would deny new methods silently, and the first symptom would be a phone
app missing a feature nobody remembered to route.

`update.apply` is the only mutating call permitted, and a test asserts that. It
still has to pass updaterd's own peer policy, so leaving btd's uid out of
`allow_uids` is a safe default: BLE can then read everything and change nothing.
Refused, each for a stated reason: select/pin (operator surgery), rollback (the
engine reverts on its own; recovery mode §8.2 should reopen it deliberately),
resetToGolden (factory reset in all but name — never over a radio), and
updaterd's private questions to robotd.

`bluer` and tokio are deliberately absent from Cargo.toml. BlueZ is Linux-only,
so the backend must sit behind a trait with a fake as duck-control does for the
Dynamixel bus. More awkwardly, `bluer` links libdbus and the release pipeline
cross-compiles for aarch64 — a C dependency needs a sysroot CI does not have, so
that is a build-system change to weigh against a pure-Rust D-Bus client (zbus,
already the likely choice for configd), not a dependency to add casually.

`net.*` and `system.*` are not routed yet because `configd` does not exist. When
it does they are one arm each and nothing else here changes — which is the design
claim this slice exists to make good on.

One measured constraint for the backend: BLE is not usable on this board until
~73s after power-on, because `aic-bluetooth.service` brings hci0 up late. So
whatever drives the adapter must wait and retry for one rather than assume it at
startup — the same shape as robotd waiting for the motor bus.

14 tests, no hardware.

btd: the BLE service, end to end but for the radio

Completes the front door begun in the previous commit: a session proxy, the
BlueZ backend, the daemon binary and its unit.

`link` is the seam, and it is deliberately **not a trait**. A GattLink trait
would need an async recv and an async send, and the session loop waits on both
at once — which means either splitting the link into halves with associated
types or fighting the borrow checker inside a select!. Two channels and a plain
struct say the same thing, and the tests construct one instead of implementing
anything.

`session` is the whole of the behaviour, and it forwards each request
**verbatim**. It parses a line only far enough to answer two questions — is this
method allowed here, and which socket owns it — then passes the original bytes
on. It never rewrites `id`, never re-serialises params, never invents a result.
That is what keeps btd a transport rather than a second implementation of the
API, and it is why a subscription's notification stream needs no special case:
replies and notifications are both just lines to forward.

`upstream` holds one connection per service, opened on demand. Lazily, because
most sessions touch one service and a dead robotd should not delay a session
that never needed it. Every operation is timeout-bounded, and a broken pipe drops
the connection so the next call reconnects rather than writing into a dead socket
forever.

`bluez` uses bluer's **IO model** rather than its callback model. The callback
model hands you a notifier with no way to tell which central subscribed, so
pairing a subscription to the session that should feed it means guessing — a
single global slot, which a second phone breaks. The IO model reports
device_address() on both halves, so a connection is a real duplex stream and
several centrals cost nothing. It waits and retries for an adapter rather than
exiting, because hci0 does not exist until ~73s after power-on on this board.

The unit runs btd as its own unprivileged user with SupplementaryGroups=robot,
which reaches the 0660 sockets but confers no right to change software —
mutating calls additionally need allow_uids in updater.toml, so leaving btd out
is a safe default where BLE reads everything and changes nothing. Sandboxing is
tighter than robotd can manage, since this process touches no hardware:
ProtectSystem=strict, RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX, empty
CapabilityBoundingSet.

Two gaps stated rather than hidden:

  - The request characteristic does NOT require encryption yet. §7 wants pairing
    plus encryption on anything carrying wifi credentials, and the flag is one
    line — but setting it without deciding how a phone is allowed to bond yields
    a robot nobody can provision. It goes on in the change that settles pairing,
    and before net.connect is routed.
  - Whether the `bluetooth` group is enough for a session-less daemon to reach
    org.bluez differs between images and is unverified on ours. If btd logs a
    D-Bus permission error, the fix is a policy drop-in, not running as root.

21 tests, no hardware: seven drive a whole session over real unix sockets,
including a refused call never reaching the daemon, robot.* routing to robotd
rather than updaterd, and every notification of a subscription stream arriving
through a 23-byte MTU.

Verified for the target with `cargo board --bins -p btd` — the bluer backend
type-checks against the real API for aarch64, with vendored libdbus linking
through zig cc. It has never met a radio.

configd: wifi and the robot's identity

The service `btd` was missing. `net.*` and `system.*` — scan, connect, forget,
status, name, reboot — served over a fifth unix socket.

A separate service rather than part of robotd, because config must be reachable
when the robot is dead: provisioning wifi is exactly what a client needs when
things are broken (architecture.md §3.1). And not part of btd, because btd owns
nothing (§4.1) — an SDK should not have to go through Bluetooth to set a name.

It stores NO credentials. NetworkManager owns those, persists them root-only and
reconnects by itself, so a PSK passes through configd and is forgotten. What
configd owns is a small file holding the robot's name.

The protocol carries the distinction that justified choosing NetworkManager over
netplan: `ConnectFailure::BadKey`. "You typed the password wrong" is the most
common provisioning failure there is, and netplan cannot report it — `netplan
apply` says "config applied" whether or not association succeeded. NM reports it
as device state reason 7, and the mapping from NM's reasons is tested.

`NetConnectParams` has a hand-written `Debug` that redacts the passphrase, with a
test asserting the key never reaches `{:?}` and a second asserting it still
reaches the wire. Every other params struct derives Debug; a derived one here
would put a customer's wifi password in the journal the first time any service
logged a request it could not handle.

configd runs as root, which this repo otherwise avoids. The reason is narrow:
NetworkManager's connection-modify and logind's Reboot are both polkit-gated,
there is no polkit on this image, and systemd denies both to a session-less
non-root caller. The alternative was installing a JS policy engine to authorise
two calls. The trust boundary stays in the right place — btd, which parses bytes
from anyone in radio range, is unprivileged, and configd only ever sees typed
JSON over a peer-credentialled socket. Unlike robotd it touches no hardware, so
the unit can sandbox it properly: ProtectSystem=strict, one writable path,
AF_UNIX only, empty CapabilityBoundingSet. CAP_SYS_BOOT is deliberately absent —
logind performs the reboot, configd only asks, and a capability here would allow
the unclean reboot(2) this exists to avoid.

`system.reboot` answers *before* rebooting, after a 3s delay. A daemon that
rebooted inside the call would drop the connection before responding, and every
client would have to treat a broken pipe as success.

The store is a file plus flock and rename(2), not a service (§3.1) — no single
point of failure, readable when anything is down, and the updater never touches
it so it survives an update *and* a rollback. Names are trimmed, stripped of
control characters and truncated to 24 chars on a character boundary; the stored
name is returned so a client displays what the robot has rather than what it
sent. A missing or corrupt file yields the hostname rather than refusing to
start.

btd routes all seven methods, and the exhaustive match in route.rs did its job:
adding them to the protocol broke btd's build until someone decided. Provisioning
is the case BLE exists for — a robot that has never seen a network cannot be
configured over that network — so all seven are permitted, and the test naming
which mutating calls BLE may make grew from one entry to five.

API_VERSION 2 -> 3.

33 tests, no hardware and no D-Bus: 14 in configd against an in-memory wifi stack
that can produce a wrong-key failure on demand, 19 in the protocol. Cross-checked
for the target with `cargo board --bins -p configd`, so the zbus proxies
type-check against aarch64. Never run against a real NetworkManager.

btctl: a BLE client for a laptop

The phone app's stand-in, and the only way to test btd against a real radio.

An **example, not a binary**, so btleplug never reaches the robot: an example's
dependencies are dev-dependencies and nothing here is in the shipped artifact.
btleplug rather than bluer because this half runs on a developer's machine —
CoreBluetooth on macOS, BlueZ on Linux, WinRT on Windows — and bluer would make
the client Linux-only, which defeats the point of having one.

It reuses `btd::framing`, which is the interesting part: the chunking here is the
*client* half of the same module the robot uses, so an asymmetric framing would
simply not work. That makes it a test of the protocol rather than a
reimplementation free to agree with itself.

Writing it surfaced two real design flaws the compiler found:

  - The GATT UUIDs lived in `bluez.rs`, which is `cfg(target_os = "linux")`, so a
    client could not reach them off-Linux. They are a wire contract exactly like
    the method names in duck-ipc-proto — every client must know them — so they
    move to `gatt.rs` with no platform gate, and `uuid` becomes an unconditional
    dependency.
  - `FramingError` implemented neither Display nor Error, so `?` did not work on
    it. Fine inside a binary, wrong for a library other code uses.

Also fixes updaterd, whose own exhaustive match over `Call` broke when the
protocol grew — the same protection btd has. It now names configd for net.* and
system.*, as it already named robotd for robot.*.

The whole workspace passes and every binary cross-compiles for aarch64.

robotctl net/system, and a PIN-based pairing process

Two things, plus a bug the compiler found.

## robotctl net / robotctl system

The on-robot client for configd's methods, so someone on the board is not
reduced to hand-writing JSON at a socket. `net status|scan|connect|forget` and
`system info|set-name|pin|set-pin|reboot`, each with `--json`.

Three details that are not obvious:

  - `net connect --psk-stdin` reads the passphrase from stdin, because an
    argument is visible in `ps` for the lifetime of the command and this one is a
    credential. Only the trailing newline is stripped: a passphrase may
    legitimately end in a space, and trimming one produces a wrong-password
    failure nobody could explain.
  - A failed join exits REFUSED with the reason spelled out — "the passphrase was
    rejected" — because that is the distinction NetworkManager was chosen for and
    a script wants to detect it.
  - `system reboot` refuses without `--yes`, and refuses *before* connecting, so
    a robot is not disturbed by a command the operator then aborts.

## Pairing, as a process rather than a guarantee

A six-digit PIN, stored by configd, answered to BlueZ by a bluer agent in btd.
Because the bond is made with passkey entry rather than just-works, the link is
authenticated and encrypted, which is what makes `encrypt_authenticated_write` on
the characteristic mean something — so §7's requirement for wifi credentials is
now satisfied by a mechanism rather than a comment.

Six digits, not five: Bluetooth's passkey entry is defined as a six-digit value,
000000-999999, and BlueZ hands an agent exactly that. Five would have to be
padded somewhere, and the two sides would then disagree about whether the PIN is
"12345" or "012345" — a support call nobody can diagnose. Stored as a *string*
because leading zeros are significant; a u32 would render "012345" as "12345".

The factory PIN is 000000 and is public in this repository, so out of the box this
proves physical presence and nothing more — the same guarantee just-works gives.
The difference is that the storage, the agent and the six-digit contract are all
in place, so making it a real secret is a provisioning change rather than a
redesign. `PairingPinResult::is_default` exists so every client can say out loud
that this PIN is not a secret, and robotctl does.

The PIN is deliberately NOT routed to BLE, and that refusal is the one in route.rs
that is load-bearing rather than cautious: a passkey an unpaired peer could read —
or worse, overwrite — would make pairing theatre. btd reads it over the unix
socket instead, per pairing request rather than cached, so `set-pin` takes effect
on the next pairing rather than the next reboot. A configd that cannot answer
means the bond is *refused*: falling back to the default would let anyone pair
whenever configd was briefly unreachable.

`--insecure-no-pairing` exists for bench work and says what it costs in its help
text.

Still undecided, and stated rather than implied: there is no pairing *window* — the
robot is pairable whenever it advertises, and a button-held window needs a button
that does not exist yet — and nothing revokes a bond.

## The bug

`cargo board` warned that RESPONSE_UUID was unused, which was not lint noise. The
IO-model backend serves ONE characteristic doing both write and notify, while
gatt.rs still declared two and btctl looked for both — so the client would have
failed with "no response characteristic" on its first real connection, and only
against hardware.

Unified on one characteristic carrying both directions, which is what the IO model
naturally gives: BlueZ reports a write and a subscription as separate events, and
with two characteristics they must be matched across them by address instead of
belonging to the same characteristic by construction.

Verified end to end against a real configd over a real socket: scan, a rejected
passphrase, a successful join reporting its address, the saved flag appearing,
a five-digit PIN refused, 012345 stored with its leading zero intact, a long name
truncated to 24 characters, and reboot refused without --yes.

340 tests pass, clippy is clean, and every binary cross-compiles for aarch64 with
no warnings.

Make the new daemons actually run on a board

Everything so far built the two services without installing or authorising them.
Three gaps, one of which was a real bug.

## BLE provisioning was denied

configd's peer policy permits its own uid plus whatever is listed, and its unit
listed nothing — so only root could mutate. btd runs as user `btd`, and
SO_PEERCRED reports only a peer's *primary* gid, so `SupplementaryGroups=robot`
got btd through the socket's 0660 mode and no further. Every mutating call over
Bluetooth — net.connect, system.setName, system.reboot — returned
PERMISSION_DENIED, while everything read-only worked, which is the worst shape for
a bug like this: it reads as a mystery rather than a configuration error.

configd now takes `--allow-user` and `--allow-group` by *name* rather than the
numeric `--allow-uid`/`--allow-gid` it had, resolved through getpwnam/getgrnam at
startup. systemd-sysusers allocates dynamically, so a number that is right on the
board it was written for is wrong on the next one. An unresolvable name is a
warning rather than fatal: a robot missing an optional user still serves
everything read-only.

configd.service passes `--allow-user btd` and nothing else. Note what it does not
do: it never grants the `robot` group as a whole, so being able to *talk* to
configd and being able to *reconfigure* the robot stay separate layers (§2.2).

## Nothing installed the services

install.sh now installs configd.service and btd.service, creates the btd system
user, and stops both on a forced re-install. btd is allowed to fail without
failing the install: it needs an adapter, hci0 does not exist until ~73s after
boot on this board, and a robot with no working radio still updates and walks.

## on_apply, and a test that was right

Adding both daemons to the restart set broke
`config::shipped_config_is_safe_for_a_client_robot`, which already refused to let
btd appear there. The test was right and I had not thought it through: btd may be
the *transport the update was requested over*, so restarting it drops the BLE
connection carrying `update.subscribe` — the phone that started the update loses
the progress stream and never learns the outcome. That is the whole app-driven
flow. Same class of reason updaterd does not restart itself.

So the set is `["robotd", "configd"]`. btd keeps running the old binary until the
next reboot, which is expected rather than a fault, exactly as §8.3 describes for
updaterd. configd *is* restarted: no long-lived session state, and the progress
stream a client watches comes from updaterd rather than from it.

`robotctl version` reports configd and warns if it lags, since configd is in the
restart set and so should already be current. btd is deliberately absent from that
report: it serves no socket, so there is nothing to ask it, and every crate shares
one version line. "Is btd running" is `systemctl status btd`, a different question.

340 tests pass, clippy clean, install.sh shellcheck clean, every binary
cross-compiles for aarch64 with no warnings.

Untested and belongs in board-test.sh: that configd *refuses* a mutating call from
an unauthorised peer. The allow path is verified; the deny path needs two uids and
so needs the board.

board-test: cover configd's authorisation, and name failed units

The security property this whole BLE path rests on had no test anywhere: that
configd *refuses* a mutating call from a peer that may talk to it but is not
allowed to change it. The unit tests can only reach the allow path, because the
deny path needs two uids and a real unix socket — so board-test.sh is the only
place it can be asserted at all, and it already had the pattern for it.

Eleven checks, following the layered-access ones updaterd has:

  - the socket is root:robot 0660, which is what makes `Group=robot` in the unit
    mean "the robot group" rather than "root only"
  - `--allow-user` resolves a name to a uid at startup, which is the property that
    lets a shipped unit say `btd` on a board where sysusers allocated a different
    number
  - a group member can read; a non-member is blocked by the socket mode (exit 3)
  - the *named* user may change configuration — the property `--allow-user btd`
    relies on, and without which every provisioning call over BLE is refused
  - a second group member that is NOT named is denied (exit 6), and the refused
    rename did not take effect. Reaching the daemon and being allowed to change it
    stay separate permissions, which is the whole two-tier design (§2.2)
  - a rejected passphrase exits 5 rather than 1, so a script can tell "wrong
    password" from "could not ask" — the outcome NetworkManager was chosen for
  - a PIN keeps its leading zero, because the two sides of a pairing must agree on
    six characters and a u32 would render 012345 as 12345
  - the passphrase is not in the log, checked against the shipped binary rather
    than against the type in isolation
  - `btd --version` runs on the target, which is a real cross-link check: btd is
    the only binary pulling C beyond zstd, since bluer links libdbus built from
    vendored source by zig cc, and a dynamic-linker or glibc-floor problem there
    is invisible on the build host

"No failed units" went to setup-board.sh instead of here, because board-test.sh
runs in a container with no systemd and the check would be vacuous. It exists
because `systemd-networkd-wait-online` failed on every boot of this board for a
week, cost 20s each time, delayed updaterd behind network-online.target, and
nothing reported it.

Verified locally as far as a macOS host allows: `btd --version` runs, a rejected
passphrase exits 5, the PIN round-trips with its leading zero, and the journal
records `psk: "<redacted>"` with the SSID intact. The container checks themselves
are unverified until CI — there is no Docker on this machine — though the script
passes `sh -n` and shellcheck with no findings beyond the one SC2016 that was
already there.

The app may update the robot, and pairing is the PIN alone

Two decisions, recorded in code and in the tests that keep them.

## An owner may start an update from their phone

`update.apply` over Bluetooth returned PERMISSION_DENIED, because updaterd's
change authority was root-only. That was the safe default while btd did not
exist; btd exists now, and M6's headline is a non-developer updating the robot
from the phone.

deploy/updater.toml now says `allow_users = ["btd"]`. Note how narrow the claim
is: "btd may relay an update request from the app", not "anything in the robot
group may replace the firmware". Reaching the socket and being allowed to change
the robot stay separate permissions.

By name, not by uid, and updaterd gained the same name resolution configd has:
systemd-sysusers allocates dynamically, so a number written into a shipped config
is right on the board it was written for and wrong on the next one. The numeric
`allow_uids`/`allow_gids` remain for a bench override.

`shipped_config_is_safe_for_a_client_robot` changed from "grant nobody" to three
sharper assertions: the shipped config grants by name and never by number, `btd`
must be present or the phone button is dead, and `allow_groups` must never contain
`robot` — which is the layering the whole design rests on.

The resolver is duplicated between updaterd and configd rather than shared. The
obvious home would be duck-ipc-proto, and that crate is types only: every service
speaks it, including the ones on the recovery path, so it may not grow a libc
dependency for two callers.

## Pairing is the PIN, and there is no button

Recorded as a decision rather than left as an open question. A per-robot PIN
already carries what a pairing window would add: if it is unique and printed under
the robot, knowing it requires physical access, and anyone who can read the sticker
can pick the robot up. A window would only defend against someone in range while
the factory default is still in place, and the answer to that is a real PIN.

A button would add a visible consent moment, a recovery path when the PIN is lost,
and defence in depth if a sticker is photographed. None is needed for v1, and each
stays additive: an enclosure with a button can gate `set_pairable` without changing
anything here.

The consequence is that security rests entirely on the PIN being per-robot, which
makes it a provisioning obligation rather than a software one — something must
generate it, print it, and record what was printed. That is updater-design.md
§5.7's per-device state, the same slot that owes us a serial number, and two things
wanting one home is a reason to define it once.

340 tests pass, clippy clean, aarch64 cross-compiles with no warnings. The name
resolution in updaterd is the same code verified in configd; the shipped config is
asserted by test rather than by hand.

docs: the app path, and three claims the board disproved

Everything about btd and configd lived in commit messages, which is the wrong
place: a commit message is found by someone who already knows what they are
looking for.

## docs/app-path-design.md

btd and configd in one document rather than two, because they are one feature and
every decision in one constrains the other: btd owns nothing, so configd exists;
configd serves a PIN, so btd can pair; a method routed in btd is a method configd
must answer. Named for the roadmap's own term for it.

It records the decisions and, more usefully, the alternatives that were rejected
and why — per-field GATT characteristics, two characteristics instead of one,
driving wpa_supplicant directly, a pairing window, a trait instead of channels for
the radio seam. Sections established on the board rather than reasoned about are
marked `measured`, and §6.1 says plainly what is not tested: neither service has
met a radio or a real NetworkManager, and the netplan cutover runs only on a
freshly flashed board.

## Three claims that were wrong

architecture.md §3 said clients drive NetworkManager over D-Bus, as though a board
had NetworkManager. It does not — Armbian's headless image is netplan +
systemd-networkd + wpa_supplicant. The decision stands and now says why it stands
against what the image actually ships, plus the finding that made it non-obvious:
the D-Bus-enabled wpa_supplicant instance holds no interface at all, so driving it
directly would mean displacing netplan anyway, with none of NM's failure reporting.

§1.1 listed btd and updaterd as surviving a dead robotd. configd belongs there for
a concrete reason rather than symmetry: provisioning wifi is exactly what someone
needs when the robot is broken.

§3.1 described the config store as unbuilt. It exists, holds the name and the
pairing PIN, and deliberately has no inotify yet — that earns its place when a
second process reads the file.

## Two roadmap questions the board already answered

M4 asked whether Armbian's RAM-log puts /var/log on tmpfs. It does: var-log.mount
sits on dev-zram1, so Storage=persistent is a directory in memory, and the update
history under /var/lib really is the only durable record. Recorded in
deploy/README.md too, next to the drop-in it qualifies.

M4 also wanted a real boot measurement for the 30s health-gate timeout. 1m43s, and
the gate is not paying it: the critical path is zram, an 11.7s journal flush, dbus
blocked for 26.4s, then NetworkManager — gated behind the out-of-tree aic8800
driver, which is why hci0 does not exist until ~73s and why btd waits for an
adapter rather than exiting. on_apply restarts robotd rather than rebooting, so 30s
stands; a reboot-based recovery path would need several times that.

## Also

M6 records that btd and configd landed early and what that leaves. Provisioning
moved from "deciding nothing now is fine" to a blocking item, because BLE pairing
security rests on a per-robot PIN that nothing generates yet. deploy/README.md
grew the migration as step 2 of three. README and the crate tree name both new
services and stop calling them unbuilt.

Two new open questions in §9: bond revocation, and the per-device provisioning slot
now having two claimants — the serial and the PIN — which is a reason to define it
once.

Every internal link checked; 340 tests still pass.

Merge main: slice 2's intents, and BLE refuses all of them

18 commits, and the interesting part of the merge was not the textual conflicts.

## btd's exhaustive match earned itself a third time

Slice 2 added robot.move, robot.head, robot.stop, robot.enable and
robot.subscribe. btd would not compile until each was decided, which is what that
match is for. All five are refused, and the reasoning is in the file:

  - move/head/enable are motor control, and §4.1's "subset" is precisely about
    this. Teleop belongs on WebRTC's unreliable `teleop` datachannel, where a
    stale command is dropped rather than retransmitted (§5.2). A 20-byte
    notification budget on a link that does not exist for the first ~73s of a boot
    is not a control transport.
  - robot.stop got its own arm because refusing it looks wrong. An emergency stop
    in the app is exactly what someone reaches for — but a stop button over an
    unbonded, high-latency, sometimes-absent radio is worse than no button,
    because it *looks* like an e-stop and is not one. robotd's deadman already
    stops the robot when intents stop arriving, and that does not depend on a
    phone being in range. A real e-stop is physical. Reconsider deliberately, with
    the caveat stated in the UI, if the app ever needs it.
  - robot.subscribe streams state at up to the control rate. Over BLE a client

        _ => Err(ReqError::NotSupported.into()),

benefit that does not exist. The IO model reports `device_address()` on both
halves, which looked necessary to pair a subscription with the session that should

once you read it arithmetically:

    ← error -32700 "missing field `method` at line 1 column 39"

That request is 60 bytes, so three 20-byte chunks. Reassembling chunks 1 and 3
without 2 gives `{"id":1,"jsonrpc":"2.info","params":{}}` — 39 characters, valid

chunks can swap places. A reordered chunk does not fail — it silently reassembles

client sending malformed JSON.

order is preserved. A full queue refuses the write rather than dropping the chunk,
because a refused write is recoverable — the client resends the request — and a
corrupted line is not.

The PIN design assumed something BLE cannot do, and hardware said so: macOS
displayed its own random six-digit code and waited for someone to type it into a
robot with no keyboard.

In LE passkey entry one side displays and the other inputs, and the roles follow
from the IO capabilities each side declares. Implementing `request_passkey` declared
"this device can input", so macOS took the display role. The reverse is no better:
with `DisplayPasskey` the spec has the *displaying* side generate the passkey, so
BlueZ chooses it and a stored value cannot be presented — and a headless robot has
nothing to display it on regardless. A fixed printed PIN is simply not expressible
in BLE passkey entry. That should have been checked against the spec before the agent
was written.

So the check moves up a layer, which is the option that keeps everything the PIN work
already built:

  - Pairing is just-works: every agent handler None, which bluer publishes as
    NoInputNoOutput. The read on the characteristic requires `encrypt_read` — plain,
    not `encrypt_authenticated_*`, because a just-works bond can never satisfy the
    authenticated variants and demanding them would refuse every client that pairs.
  - `btd` then serves nothing until `system.authenticate` passes. That call is
    answered by the transport rather than forwarded, so the routing table gains a
    third outcome, `Route::Local`, alongside forward and refuse.
  - `hello` is the one other call allowed through, because it reports only versions —
    what the GATT read already tells an unauthenticated client — and refusing it
    would leave a mismatched client unable to learn why nothing works.

Three attempts, then the session closes: a six-digit PIN is a million guesses over a
link that is encrypted but not authenticated, so rationing is the only thing making
brute force expensive, and reconnecting costs a full bond. `attempts_remaining` goes
back to the client so it can say "two left" rather than silently losing its
connection.

The PIN is fetched per attempt rather than cached, so `set-pin` takes effect on the
next try; a configd that cannot answer refuses the session rather than admitting it.

test for that specifically.

API_VERSION 3 -> 4, because a v3 client would otherwise have every call refused with
no idea why. `AuthenticateParams` redacts its PIN in Debug, like NetConnectParams.

btd: size a reply for the link, and stop calling a full queue a disconnect

`duckctl logs robotd` was the first reply big enough to find this. Measured
against the board: a ~5 KiB tail (≈265 notifications at the 20-byte floor)
arrives in 1.83 s, and a ~7 KiB one (≈350) tears the notification session down
150 ms in. `btd` logged one INFO line saying the central had unsubscribed — it
had not, CoreBluetooth still had the link up — and the client sat waiting out a
60-second idle budget holding half an answer, with nothing anywhere to blame.

Two faults, both in the notify pump, and neither specific to logs: any reply
this size hits them, which is also why `update.show` was never usable from a
laptop.

**A full queue is not a departed central.** `bluer`'s `notify` returns the same
`NotificationSessionStopped` for "the central unsubscribed" and "the D-Bus
connection would not take this signal", and the pump read both as the central
leaving — so a reply too big for one burst ended the session mid-line. Only
`is_stopped()` distinguishes them. A chunk is now retried five times over
100 ms, and only a genuinely stopped session or an exhausted budget ends things;
giving up says so at `warn` instead of `debug`, since the old line was invisible
under `RUST_LOG=info` and the one that *was* visible blamed the client.

**The payload comes from the write side now.** The notify side cannot ask BlueZ
what the link negotiated — that has not changed, and `bluer`'s IO model, which
has both an MTU and a real `sendable()`, still serves only the `Acquire*` paths
a CoreBluetooth central never drives (bf0d5f9). But BlueZ reports the MTU on
every inbound *write*, one ATT MTU serves both directions, and a central always
writes before there is anything to send back: `system.authenticate` is the first
write of every session. So `Link` carries a shared cell instead of a number, a
session opens at the 20-byte floor, and every reply after that first write is
sized for the real link — roughly a tenfold cut in notifications. Read once per
line, never per chunk, because a line chunked two ways cannot be reassembled.

**And the pump paces itself**, sixteen chunks then about a connection interval,
because `notify` hands a signal to the connection and returns rather than
waiting for the radio. That is a workaround for a missing readiness signal
rather than flow control, and it is labelled as one.

`DEFAULT_TURN_ENDPOINT` pointed at `turn.fastrtc.org`, which `fastrtc`'s own
code points at and `reachy_mini` #1182 copied. That name is a dangling
delegation rather than an outage: the `.org` registry names four Route53

and all four nameservers answer REFUSED for the zone they are authoritative
for — what Route53 says when the hosted zone behind them is gone. The Space
that alias pointed at, `fastrtc/turn-service`, never stopped answering.

So address it directly. Every microduck robot has been offering host and srflx
candidates only, which is why a consumer behind symmetric NAT or CGNAT could
not reach one at all, and why demos passed regardless: two peers on one
network pair on host candidates and never look at a relay.

It also takes a name that can be taken over out of the path a signed-in robot
sends its account token down. A dangling Route53 delegation is a known takeover
shape, and whoever landed one of those four nameservers would serve records for
the name, pass DNS validation for a certificate on it, and be handed the token
every five minutes.

`turn::parse_endpoint` checks `--turn-url` before the token can reach it —
https unless the host is loopback, no userinfo, no query, no fragment — as a

instead of becoming a warning every thirty seconds. Redirects need no guard:
`reqwest` strips `Authorization` when one crosses scheme, host or port.

of them used it as the justification for a design. `stream.rs` still sends
frames outbound and `lan.py` is still a LAN transport, but for the reason that
was always the real one — a relay is metered against the robot owner's
allowance, and the shortest path between a board and a data centre is not
through a third one — rather than because the relay was down.

connectivity check, without which nothing here would notice the endpoint dying

§6 argued that only the robot needs to offer a relay candidate: a connection
needs one and not two, and `aiortc`'s TURN client does not work, so a Python
consumer can never be that side. Both halves are true. The conclusion assumed
something it did not check — that the two ends can address each other at all.

An iPhone on a mobile network cannot. It has no IPv4 socket: it reaches a
hostname through DNS64/NAT64, the STUN server reports an IPv4 reflexive address
back, and the phone gathers a candidate saying so. But an ICE candidate is a
bare literal, and the robot's relay candidate is a bare IPv4 literal on a board
with no global IPv6 at all, which that phone cannot send a packet to.

Measured on olducky over 4G: six sessions, `offering relay candidates relays=5`
every one, `Ice connection state ... failed` every one, eight seconds apart.
The same symptom a missing relay gives, and a different cause — which is why
the robot-side endpoint fix did not move it.

So the page mints credentials for itself. Only its own allocation bridges this:
`turn.cloudflare.com` is a name, so it resolves over IPv6, and the relayed
address Cloudflare hands back is IPv4, which the robot can reach. Confirmed
from the phone before this was written — those same credentials in a Trickle
ICE page gathered a `relay` candidate with an IPv4 address over 4G, where the
robot's own candidates had paired with nothing.

With the visitor's token rather than the robot's, which is the right way round
twice: a robot's allowance should go on being watched rather than on watching,
and a browser signed in with `hf_oauth` already holds a token of its own.

`refreshRelays` runs on the connect path, which is already asynchronous and
already says "connecting…". `newPeerConnection` reads what it stored and never
fetches — the same rule the robot follows in `consumer-added`, and for the same
